demo.heading: Buy now or wait?
demo.intro: Pick a route, cabin, and departure date to see the predicted price if bought on the reference date, its {model.interval.level}% prediction interval, and a recommendation.
demo.basis: For each route and cabin, the prediction uses the one flight observed most often recently. The values were computed in advance, without a model server.

why.IMMINENT: Departure is very close. Buying now is the better choice.
why.PAST_OPTIMAL: The predicted lowest point ({v.globalBestDay} days before departure) has already passed. For the remaining days, now is predicted to be the cheapest.
why.AT_LOW: Today's price is the predicted low. Waiting will likely cost more.
why.SMALL_SAVING: The gap to the predicted low {v.bestDay} days before departure is {v.savingPct|fixed1}%, within the model's error range. Buying now makes little difference.
why.FALLING: The price is falling. It may be worth watching for {v.waitDays} more days: the predicted low is about ₩{v.bestPrice} ({v.savingPct|fixed1}% below now).
why.LATER_LOW: Buying {v.bestDay} days before departure (in about {v.waitDays} days) is predicted to save about ₩{v.saving} ({v.savingPct|fixed1}%).

demo.noForecast: There is no representative flight for this route and cabin, so there is no prediction.
demo.noJs: The demo needs JavaScript to run.

about.heading: About
about.education: B.S. in Computer Software, The University of Suwon · Expected {profile.graduation|month}
about.body1: I automated daily collection of Korea–Japan airfare prices and built a price forecasting model from that data.
about.body2: I checked whether the evaluation method was right before trusting the score, and in the process corrected an inflated R² twice.
about.body3: Alongside each prediction, it also shows the range that can be trusted.

skills.collection: Collection automation — GitHub Actions collects prices daily and auto-commits the CSV
skills.modeling: Time series modeling — per-route NeuralProphet trend + XGBoost residual learning, tuned with Optuna over {model.optunaTrials} trials
skills.validation: Validation design — checked for leakage by comparing TimeSeriesSplit, GroupKFold, and K-Fold
skills.interval: Prediction interval calibration — the {model.interval.level}% interval's actual coverage is {model.interval.coverage}%

project.heading: Korea–Japan airfare: when should you buy?
project.body: I collected airfares between Incheon and Tokyo/Osaka every day and built a model that forecasts prices by departure date and whether to buy now or wait.

data.body1: I collected airfare prices for {data.routes} routes between Incheon and Tokyo (Narita, Haneda) and Osaka (Kansai), from {data.collectStart|date} to {data.collectEnd|date}.
data.body2: Results come from the Google Flights search via SerpApi, run daily by GitHub Actions. Of {data.rawRows} raw rows, {data.filteredRows} remained after filtering out errors.
data.sparse: The closer the departure, the more often it was collected: within a week, Wednesday, Friday and Sunday departures every day; within a month, every weekday in a three-day rotation; further out, only alternate Fridays and Sundays plus holidays, once a week on Sundays. That is why the far end is sparse. The schedule changed twice early on; this is the final one.
data.heading: The data

steps.schedule: GitHub Actions · daily (far-off dates on Sundays)
steps.join: KRW/JPY rate · Korea/Japan holidays · oil price

features.model: NeuralProphet · XGBoost · Optuna · quantile regression · SHAP
features.heading: {model.featureCount} FEATURES
features.lead: What goes into predicting a single price. Percentages are each group's share of importance in the model (XGBoost gain).
features.lookupNote: Lookup importance is inflated because it shares route and airline information. On unseen departure dates these statistics fall back to defaults — something the validation step uncovered.
features.hint: Hover over a group (tap on phones) to see its feature names.

depart.body1: What moves prices more is when you fly, not when you buy. Each dot is one departure date; the higher it sits, the pricier it is than the route-and-class average. Averages by weekday are shown alongside. Dates around holidays (amber) and Sunday departures are the most expensive.
depart.heading: Price by departure date
depart.alt: Dot chart of price by departure date: departure dates across, price versus the route-and-class average up the side, with weekday averages alongside. Dates around Christmas, New Year's Day and Seollal rise the highest; among weekdays, Sunday is the most expensive.

curve.body1: I tracked prices day by day for {model.realizedFlights} flights that had already departed. Right before departure ({model.bookingCurve.0.label}), prices ran {model.bookingCurve.0.pct|signed}% above the same flight's average, while the {model.bookingCurve.5.label} window was cheapest at {model.bookingCurve.5.pct|signed}%. That's a U-shaped curve about {model.curveWidth}pp wide.
curve.heading: The U-shaped booking curve
curve.alt: Observations stacked by days-to-departure range, relative to the same flight's average. The line through the range averages forms a U.
curve.tip: Buying at {v.bin}: {v.pct} vs. same-flight average · {v.n} observations

bubble.heading: Deflating the R² bubble
bubble.body1: The first R² of {model.bubble.firstR2} I got was inflated by high-priced rows mismatched on the Haneda route. Filtering those rows out brought R² down to {model.bubble.firstR2After}, while MAE barely changed.
bubble.body2: The same thing happened again: I found and removed {data.removedImplausible} rows labeled nonstop but actually connecting flights. MAE barely changed, from ₩{model.bubble.maeBefore} to ₩{model.bubble.maeAfter}, while R² alone dropped from {model.bubble.r2Before} to {model.bubble.r2After}. Those rows made up {model.bubble.denomShare}% of the R² denominator.
bubble.body3: So I don't look at R² alone — I check it together with MAE and data integrity. Because the filter conditions differ, I don't compare this R² directly with earlier ones.

validation.heading: Validation design
validation.body1: I evaluated the same model three ways. TimeSeriesSplit, which matches production conditions, is the headline figure.
validation.body2: Evaluating on unseen departure dates with GroupKFold revealed a train/serve mismatch — on a new departure date, lookup statistics fall back to a default value. On those unseen departure dates, the lookup-enabled service configuration scored R² {model.gkfWithLookup.r2} and MAE ₩{model.gkfWithLookup.mae} — worse than without lookup. I retuned and compared {model.lookupVariants} lookup configurations.

band.heading: Prediction interval calibration
band.body1: Instead of a single price, I also output a {model.interval.level}% prediction interval.
band.body2: A fixed interval's actual coverage dropped to {model.interval.driftLow}% on more recent data. I adjusted the interval width to account for the shifting distribution, reaching {model.interval.coverage}% coverage on the most recent window.
band.body3: The dots in the cloud are spread inside the {model.interval.level}% prediction interval computed on the reference date for Incheon→Narita LCC. The bright dot in the middle is the predicted price; the sparser the edge, the less likely that price. Other routes are in the demo below.
band.alt: Predicted price and prediction interval per departure date drawn as a dot cloud. The bright dot in the middle is the predicted price; the wider the interval on a date, the more widely its dots spread.

limits.heading: Limitations and next steps
limits.body1: A simple baseline that just reuses the same flight's most recent observed price has an MAE of ₩{model.baselineMae}, barely different from the model's ₩{model.tss.mae}.
limits.body2: {model.reco.buyNow}% of recommendations are 'buy now.' Tracking actual prices showed that within two months of departure, waiting was on average a loss — and the model pointed the same way.
limits.body3: The next step is to beat the baseline by adding the same flight's recent observed prices as a feature.
